property_summary: For any caller that is the current owner, calling setOwner(x) sets owner to the provided argument x; the mutant that assigns tx.origin instead will sometimes set owner to tx.origin (not the provided argument) and thus violate this rule for inputs where tx.origin != _owner.

For any caller who is currently owner, after calling setOwner(x) the contract's owner equals the provided argument x; the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender instead makes owner equal the caller and thus violates this for inputs where caller != x.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling setOwner(newOwner) updates the public owner state to newOwner; the mutant omits the assignment so for some newOwner inputs the owner remains unchanged and thus violates this property.

For any caller that is the current owner and any address _owner, calling setOwner(_owner) on the correct contract returns successfully and updates the public owner to _owner; the mutant that unconditionally reverts breaks this because the call fails and owner remains unchanged for those inputs.

For any caller who is the current owner and any address _owner, calling setOwner(_owner) succeeds and updates the public owner to _owner in the correct contract; the mutant that unconditionally reverts will sometimes cause the call to fail (returning false via a caught revert) and thus owner remains unchanged.

For any address newOwner and any caller who is the current owner, calling setOwner(newOwner) either (a) succeeds and updates the public owner to newOwner, or (b) if the call reverts then the call did not succeed — i.e. the reference C always returns successfully and updates owner for owner-caller, whereas the mutant may revert (failing the call) leaving owner unchanged; we assert that when the caller is the current owner, the call must succeed (no revert) and thus owner equals the fuzzed newOwner.

After any call to setOwner(newOwner) made by the current owner, the contract's public owner must equal newOwner; the mutant inverts the onlyOwner check so the true owner cannot call setOwner and thus this property can be violated.

For all callers, when the current owner calls setOwner(newOwner) the contract's owner becomes newOwner; the mutant inverts the onlyOwner guard so the true owner cannot call setOwner and thus for some caller inputs the owner update will fail.

Invariant: only the current owner can successfully change owner via setOwner(address) — in the reference C, any call to setOwner by a non-owner will revert (so owner remains unchanged); the mutant removes the require and allows non-owners to change owner, breaking this invariant for some fuzzed caller/address.

For any caller address, the reference contract only allows setOwner to succeed when msg.sender equals the current owner (so owner never changes when called by a non-owner msg.sender); the mutant that checks tx.origin instead can be tricked via an intermediate contract call where msg.sender != tx.origin and thus allows unauthorized owner changes.

For every caller, only a direct caller who is equal to C.owner (i.e., msg.sender == owner) can change owner via setOwner; the mutant using tx.origin can be bypassed by making a call through an intermediate contract so tx.origin remains the original owner but msg.sender is the intermediary, allowing unauthorized change — the reference enforces msg.sender==owner for all admissible inputs while the mutant can be tricked for some inputs.

For every caller (msg.sender) the on-chain owner variable changes only when the immediate caller equals the current owner (i.e., setOwner succeeds iff msg.sender == owner); the mutant that uses tx.origin instead can be tricked via a malicious intermediary contract so owner can change when msg.sender != owner, violating this rule for some inputs.

For all callers (msg.sender) the genuine contract only allows setOwner to succeed when msg.sender == owner; the mutant using tx.origin permits an intermediate contract to change owner when msg.sender != owner, so there exist addresses (an intermediary contract and a newOwner) that make the mutant accept but the reference reject.

For all callers and parameters, setOwner succeeds only when msg.sender equals the current owner (so owner only changes when the immediate caller is the owner); the mutant that uses tx.origin can be made to accept a call where msg.sender != owner via an intermediate contract, breaking this rule.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling setOwner(newOwner) completes and returns true while updating owner to newOwner; the mutant returns false despite updating owner, so the return value differs for some inputs.

For any caller who is the current owner and any _owner address, calling setOwner(...) completes and the reference implementation always returns true; the mutant can return false when the stored owner equals the new owner check is observed (so mutant's return value may differ), so the mutant violates the rule for some inputs.

For any caller who is the current owner and any _owner argument, calling setOwner(_owner) on the correct contract always returns true; the mutant can return false when the stored owner equals the new owner check (owner == _owner) yields false-positive/zero-value differences, so it breaks this rule for some input.

For any caller who is the current owner and any address _owner, calling setOwner(_owner) always returns true in the reference; the mutant may return false when its return value is (owner == _owner) after assignment, so there exist inputs where the mutant's returned bool differs (false) while the reference returns true.

For any caller who is the contract owner and any address _owner, calling setOwner(_owner) always returns true in the reference; the mutant can return false when the assigned owner equals the new value check yields false (or true/false mismatch), so there exist fuzzed inputs where the mutant's returned bool differs from true.

For any caller that is the current owner and any fuzzed address _owner, calling setOwner(_owner) always returns true on the correct contract; the mutant that returns (owner == _owner) can return false for some fuzzed _owner (specifically when the assigned owner differs from the prior value in a way that makes the equality check false), so the mutant violates this universal-return-true rule for some inputs.
For any caller who is the current owner, calling setOwner(...) succeeds (does not revert) and returns true; the mutant returns false instead for those successful calls, breaking the rule.

For any caller who is the current owner and calls setOwner(newOwner), the reference contract always returns true (call completes and returns true); the mutant returns false for those successful calls, so there exist inputs (owner calling setOwner) that make the mutant violate this property.

For every caller who is the current owner, calling setOwner(_owner) succeeds and the reference always returns true while the mutant may return false when the new owner equals the caller (it returns msg.sender == _owner), so the invariant is: for any caller equal to c.owner(), calling setOwner(...) returns true; the mutant violates this for inputs where caller == _owner.

For every caller address, calling setOwner returns true only when the caller is the current owner; the mutant removing the require allows non-owners to successfully call setOwner and return true, violating this rule for some caller addresses.

Invariant: after any successful call to setOwner(x) made by the current owner, the contract's owner getter equals the exact address argument x (no change in representation); the mutant that assigns payable(_owner) can change equality due to conversion differences when steps involve address types—therefore the reference preserves exact-address equality for all inputs while the mutant can break it for some inputs.

For any address passed to setOwner by the current owner, the public owner getter of the correct contract equals the exact address value after the call; the mutant that assigns payable(_owner) can produce a different stored value when the fuzzed address is a contract address (non-zero code), so there exists some address input (a contract) for which the mutant's owner != the argument while the reference preserves equality.

For any address caller provided to setOwner when invoked by the current owner, the reference contract stores exactly that address in the public owner slot (owner getter equals the passed address); the mutant that assigns payable(_owner) can differ when the passed address is a contract address (has code) because the payable conversion on that address may produce a stored value that is not strictly equal to the uncast address value, so some contract addresses make the mutant violate this equality.

For any address x passed by the current owner to setOwner(x), the reference contract stores owner equal to x (the public getter returns the exact address); the mutant that assigns payable(_owner) can change the stored value for certain inputs (specifically when the fuzzed address is a contract address), so there exists some address input where the mutant's owner getter != the passed address while the reference always preserves equality.

For every address arg passed by the current owner to setOwner, the correct contract's public owner getter equals that exact address after the call; the mutant that casts to payable can produce a different stored value when the address has a non-zero contract code (i.e. is a contract), so there exists some contract address input for which the mutant's owner != the passed address while the reference always preserves equality.
